newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Canterbury business confidence up - survey.
newsitem.headline: Canterbury business confidence up - survey.

text.p: A major upward swing in Canterbury business confidence is under way despite short-term trading problems, according to the latest Canterbury Employers Chamber of Commerce quarterly survey.
Chamber chief executive Peter Townsend said the November survey of 501 Canterbury businesses showed that 57 percent were expecting lower interest rates, compared with just 19 percent in August.
There were 30 percent of businesses tipping improved business conditions in the next six months as against 17 percent in August, the New Zealand Press Association reported.
Townsend said the survey findings had been much more optimistic than he had expected against a background of anecdotal evidence that business conditions were tight.
"After the survey results were all checked out I rang around major key players in the Canterbury economy and they confirmed the survey findings," Townsend said.
There was a belief that if roughly the same economic settings stayed intact under a coalition government the economy would start to "fire up".
The survey showed that with a perception of falling interest rates and a continued positive economic outlook the present uncertainty over coalition talks had had limited impact so far.

The survey results also showed anticipated investment in plant and machinery rising slightly to 28 percent, compared to 24 percent in August and investment in buildings rising to 21 percent from 15 percent.
There was also optimism about domestic sales and export sales in the next three months.
The trend toward a lowering of the value of the New Zealand dollar that started late last week would fuel the perception that things would improve.

"Exporters, in particular manufacturers, and some sectors of the rural sector are suffering in tight trading conditions and the high dollar was really squeezing margins and impacting on profitability," Townsend said.
The beef and wool industries, within the rural sector, had been particularly hard hit by the exchange rate in the past year and this had combined with low world commodity prices.

A lack of demand was continuing to be the most limiting factor for Canterbury businesses with 43 percent of the group still reporting this as their major limiting factor. This compared with 50 percent in August.
Present tight conditions also showed up in a slight rise in shortage of finance which affected 20 per cent in November, compared with 17 per cent last quarter.
Employment conditions had eased slightly with 16 percent expecting to increase fulltime staff over the next quarter, down from 17 percent in August.
"Employment growth is expected to continue to slow, as businesses focus on improving productivity to retain profit margins by reducing costs and improving efficiency," said Townsend.
He warned that the business community was apprehensive about any sharp changes to economic policy settings under a new coalition government.
"The new government must make its first priority to hold a tight line on government spending and introduce competition in those sectors where costs have continued to rise, for example ACC," he said.
There was a great need for a carefully balanced range of policy initiatives to keep New Zealand's economy "on track" and to fuel business confidence.

A continued high dollar and the prospect of significant changes in policy settings could easily result in a marked shift in business confidence and performance over the next three months, Townsend said.
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
